title.official: Sending in certified record of proceedings

subdivision.heading: Additional Rules Specific to Originating Applications for Judicial Review

operative_text.controlling:
3.19(1)  On receipt of an originating application for judicial review
and a notice in accordance with rule 3.18, the person or body
named in the notice must, as soon as practicable,
(a) comply with the notice and send to the court clerk a
certified record of proceedings in Form 9, or
(b) provide in Form 9 a written explanation why the notice
cannot be complied with or fully complied with.
(2)  The certified record of proceedings sent to the court clerk
under this rule constitutes part of the court file of the originating
application.
(3)  If the Court is not satisfied with the explanation for not sending
all or part of the record of proceedings, the Court may order any or
all of the following:
(a) the person or body to provide a better explanation;
(b) the person or body to send a certified copy of a record to
the court clerk;
(c) the person or body to take any other action the Court
considers appropriate.

BOOK_B.title: Sending in certified record of proceedings

commentary.text: Rule 3.19 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.19. 1. The Return In IMS Health Canada Ltd. v. Information and Privacy Commissioner, 2005 ABCA 325, 2005 CarswellAlta 1416, 376 A.R. 336, 53 Alta. L.R. (4th) 201, Ritter J.A. discussed what must be returned under Rule 753.13. In that case, the Alberta Information and Privacy Commissioner had decided to investigate certain disclosures made by pharmacies to IMS Health Canada Ltd. (a company that collected and analyzed information concerning health care). IMS sought judicial review of the Commissioner's decision, and a dispute arose over what should be included in the Commissioner's return to the Court. At pp. 347-351, his Lordship said: Two points can be drawn from these decisions. First, “the matter” to be touched upon is the decision itself or the hearing that led to the decision. Only what was before the decision-maker at the hearing forms the return. Second, there must be a basis or reason for including a paper or document in the record. I will examine each of these propositions. 1. — What is “the matter” being touched upon? What is in issue? “The matter” is determined by what has been put in issue by the originating notice. In many instances what is in issue will be the ultimate decision made by a decision-maker. However, in some judicial reviews the substantive decisions are not the only focus of an attack; challenges can be made to procedural choices and prior, related decisions. To the extent that Broda and Robertson seem to have limited “the matter” to the ultimate decision, I disagree with that conclusion. . . . . . Support for the conclusion that “the matter” is to be determined by what an applicant has put into issue is found in Ady v. Law Society of Alberta (1994), 29 Admin. L.R. (2d) 56 (Alta. C.A.). In Ady the issue was whether the return should have included material relating to decisions made at a lower level of a chain of decision-makers. This court held that as Ady's originating motion addressed the decision of the Hearing Committee but did not request a review of the initial decision of the Conduct Committee, he was barred from “extending through the back door” any additional records relating to the prior, included decision of the Conduct Committee. At paras. 4 and 11-12 the panel stated: We note that the originating motion before the Queen's Bench asks for statutory review of the decision of the Hearing Committee to discipline Mr. Ady. It does not seek statutory review of earlier decisions by the deputy secretary or the Conduct Committee, decisions that may or may not have led to the hearing before the Hearing Committee … Mr. Ady argues that the real object of his original application was the Law Society itself, not the decision of the Hearing Committee, and that the entire matter is all one proceeding. We do not agree. His motion does not say that and, even if it did, we would be inclined to require a more specific attack. These statements suggest that had the earlier decision of the Conduct Committee been placed in issue by Ady, the return may have had to include the papers or documents required to deal with that issue. … The threshold for allegations of differential treatment Administrative decision-makers are to be granted limited deliberative secrecy: Tremblay v. Commission des affaires sociales et autre, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 952, 136 N.R. 5, 47 Q.A.C. 169. The ability to draw conclusions untrammelled by any concern of subsequent disclosure of the thought process and the ability to change those thoughts after further reflection without fear of subsequent criticism or explanation are necessary elements to decision-making: Glengarry Memorial Hospital v. Pay Equity Hearings Tribunal (Ont.) et al. (1993), 60 O.A.C. 161, 99 D.L.R. (4th) 682 (Div. Ct.); leave to appeal denied on this issue (1993), 99 D.L.R. (4th) 706 (Ont. Div. Ct.); see also Ron Ellis and Paul Atterma, Deliberative Secrecy and Adjudicative Independence: The Glengarry Precipice, (1994) 7 C.J.A.L.P. 171. These principles are relevant to an examination of the investigative decision. Deliberative secrecy is not absolute; it must be balanced with deliberative openness. To ensure that a balance is kept, simple allegations or speculation of differential treatment or unfairness are insufficient; a threshold must be met. Such a threshold must include a factual foundation for the allegation in the originating motion. Support for the use of a threshold exists in the British Columbia Court of Appeal decisions of Kuntz v. College of Physicians and Surgeons (B.C.) (1996), 73 B.C.A.C. 167, 120 W.A.C. 167, 21 B.C.L.R. (3d) 219 (C.A.) and Hammami v. College of Physicians and Surgeons (B.C.) (1996), 73 B.C.A.C. 205, 120 W.A.C. 205, 21 B.C.L.R. (3d) 267 (C.A.). In these companion cases, the court held that for a further, more comprehensive production of records for judicial review, there must be an evidentiary basis and the allegations must not be intended to “investigate the possibility”. Similarly, in Tremblay at p. 966 [S.C.R.], the Supreme Court also established a threshold for piercing the veil of deliberative secrecy: by the very nature of the control exercised over their decisions administrative tribunals cannot rely on deliberative secrecy to the same extent as judicial tribunals. Of course, secrecy remains the rule, but it may nonetheless be lifted when the litigant can present valid reasons for believing that the process followed did not comply with the rules of natural justice. In Waverley (Village Commissioners) et al. v. Kerr et al. (1994), 129 N.S.R. (2d) 298, 362 A.P.R. 298, the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal used similar wording to establish a threshold: A distinction exists between discovery, which is a somewhat unfocussed fact gathering exercise, and the examination of witnesses in the course of a judicial review, when issues are more defined and questions must be relevant to them. In either case, discovery or testimony, a proper evidentiary foundation must be created, generally by affidavit evidence, to establish that valid reasons exist for concern that there has been a want of natural justice or procedural fairness, or that the discretionary authority has been otherwise exceeded. Thus a party must show that there is a valid reason for belief in the allegation before records related to that matter must be included in the return. A valid reason for belief can be shown by affidavit. Another way in which a valid reason for belief is established is through the actions or admissions of a decision-maker. … 2. — What does “touching” the matter mean? What constitutes something which “touches” the matter? I conclude that the items which “touch” the matter are broader than the items specifically enumerated in rule 753.13(1)(a)(b) and (c). If rule 753.13(1)(d) were limited to the items specifically enumerated, the use of the term “touching the matter” would be unnecessary. The phrase “touching the matter” was originally included in rule 200(1) which allowed parties at examination for discovery to examine other parties on anything “touching the matters in question”. On November 1, 1999 this phrase was replaced with the test of relevance and materiality. In this context, there is substantial case law giving the phrase a broad and expansive meaning. In Canadian Utilities Ltd. v. Mannix Ltd. et al. (1959), 27 W.W.R. (N.S.) 508 (Alta. T.D.), at p. 521, Riley, J., held that the discovery rules permitted greater latitude than that permitted by the rules of admissibility at trial. The term “touching the matters in question” was found to be broader in scope than “material” and “relevant”. Justice Haddad took a similar approach in Czuy v. Mitchell et al. (1976), 1 A.R. 434, 72 D.L.R. (3d) 424 (C.A.), at p. 427-429. He concluded that questions which were relevant to the matters in issue or which could possibly affect the issues between the parties, were questions which touched the matters in question. Prior to 1977, British Columbia's discovery rules also contained the phrase “touching the matters in question.” Again, the phrase was broadly interpreted. Relevant questions, and even potentially relevant questions, touch the matters in question: see Hopper v. Dunsmuir (1903), 10 B.C.R. 23 (C.A.); Wismer v. Maclean-Hunter Publishing Co. and Fraser No. 2 (1953), 10 W.W.R.(N.S.) 625 (B.C.C.A.); Cominco Ltd. v. Westinghouse Canada Ltd. (1979), 11 B.C.L.R. 142 (C.A.). Other courts have also broadly interpreted similar phrases. In Saskatchewan, rule 222 permits oral discovery “touching the matters in issue in the action”. The interpretation of this phrase is consistent with that in British Columbia and Alberta. Something less than materiality or relevance is required: see R. and Minister of Highways v. Wells (W.C.) Construction Co. (1969), 72 W.W.R.(N.S.) 121 (Sask. Q.B.); Cominco Ltd. v. Phillips Cables Ltd. et al., [1987] 3 W.W.R. 562, 54 Sask.R. 134 (C.A.); Steier et al. v. University Hospital Board et al., [1988] 4 W.W.R. 303, 67 Sask. R. 81 (C.A.). In Compagnie Financière et Commerciale du Pacifique v. Peruvian Guano Co. (1882), 11 Q.B.D. 55 (C.A.), the English Court of Appeal interpreted the phrase “relating to any matter in question” in Order XXXI rule 12. The court held at p. 62-65 that the phrase included documents: … which not only would be evidence upon any issue, but also which, it is reasonable to suppose, contains information which may—not which must—either directly or indirectly enable the party requiring the affidavit to advance his own case, or to damage the case of his adversary … a document can properly be said to contain information which may enable the party requiring the affidavit to either advance his own case or to damage the case of his adversary, if it is a document which may fairly lead him to a train of inquiry… These interpretations provide some guidance. Concerns about far ranging returns are alleviated by the fact that the return is only directed at what is in issue. Moreover, in circumstances where the administrative decision-maker is insulated from investigative and other preliminary processes, the decision-maker will not possess documents relating to those functions and cannot be expected to include them in the return. Demands for more expansive returns cannot become fishing expeditions because the party attacking administrative decisions will not be granted access to the documents unless they have raised a valid reason for belief in the allegations underlying their attack. The Commissioner is required to include in his return all things which touch on the issue of his decision to conduct an investigation and to issue an order relating only to the disclosures made by pharmacists and pharmacies to IMS. 2. Transcript or Recording Must Be Forwarded The words of Rule 753.13(1) are quite broad and equally clear: “the judgment, order or decision, as the case may be, together with the process commencing the proceedings, the evidence and all exhibits filed, if any, and all things touching the matter and the notice served on him…” This is sufficiently broad to include the transcript and any evidence considered by the tribunal. If a transcript is not available, but the proceedings were mechanically or otherwise recorded, submission of such records would be sufficient to comply with the Rules. Friends of the Old Man River Society v. Assn. of Professional Engineers, Geologists & Geophysicists (Alberta) (1997), 55 Alta. L.R. (3d) 373 (Q.B.), at p. 406, per Cooke J. 3. The Meaning of “All other papers …” In Robertson v. Edmonton (City) Police Service, 2004 ABQB 243, 2004 CarswellAlta 511, 355 A.R. 281, 39 Alta. L.R. (4th) 239, Slatter J. said, at p. 298: The requirement to produce “all other papers or documents touching the matter” does not mean that the tribunal has to make full disclosure of all records in its possession or power. For the purposes of the Return the “matter” is the decision and the way it was made. Generally only documents that were actually before the decision-maker at the time the decision was made need be included: Broda v. Edmonton (City), supra, at paras. 6-12; Labour Relations Board (Alta.) v. International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local 1007 (1991), 83 Alta. L.R. (2d) 253, § 18 (Q.B.); Ady v. Law Society of Alberta (1994), 29 Admin. L.R. (2d) 56, (C.A.). 4. No Right of Examination except under the Rules In Operative Plasterers' and Cement Masons' International Association of the United States and Canada, Local 222 v. Alberta, 2007 ABQB 34, 2007 CarswellAlta 77, 413 A.R. 184, Bielby J. said, at p. 187: In the absence of a Rule of Court or other statutory authority authorizing same, the Applicants are not entitled to conduct an examination as if for discovery of the party who certified the contents of a Return filed in relation to an application for judicial review. Her Ladyship then said, at pp. 191-192: There is no requirement in the Rules of Court nor elsewhere that the Crown submit to an examination or cross-examination on the contents of a Return. The subject of the contents of the Return may be canvassed during the course of a Rule 266 examination, however.

BOOK_C.title: Sending in certified record of proceedings

commentary.text:
This rule works in conjunction with rule 3.18. It mandates the return of a Form 9 certified record of proceedings or an explanation as to why compliance is partially or fully impossible. The purpose is to obtain the record of what was before the decision-maker so that the court will have the same record as the basis for its review of the decision.
[2004] O.J. No. 4351 (Ont. Div. Ct.), when stating: “[a] record need not be produced if the body and act in question were not subject to judicial review and the time to make that determination was prior to the hearing of the full review application.”
